items.title: Xinhua Asia-Pacific news summary at 1600 GMT, Nov. 14
text: NEW DELHI -- At least 26 people were killed and many others injured Friday in a head-on collision between a minibus and a container truck in India's northeastern state of Assam, officials said.
The accident took place at Rongajan, near Kaziranga in Golaghat district, about 274 km northeast of Dispur, the capital city of Assam. (India-Traffic Accident-Deaths)

TOKYO -- A 27-year-old U.S. Air Force captain was arrested by Japanese police on Saturday in Okinawa Prefecture on suspicion of driving under the influence of alcohol, despite measures taken by the U.S. military to curb misconduct among its personnel, local media reported.

According to Kyodo News, the captain, Omena Mushale, who is assigned to Kadena Air Base, was arrested at the scene in the southern Japanese prefecture for allegedly violating Japan's road traffic law. The arrest comes as drunk-driving cases involving U.S. military personnel continue to occur. (Japan-U.S. Military-Drunk Driving)

HANOI -- Six soldiers were killed after a BMP-1 armored vehicle sank during combat-readiness training at the TB1 National Shooting Range in Vietnam's northern Bac Ninh city on Thursday, Vietnam's Ministry of National Defense said Saturday.
The vehicle encountered a problem and sank at around 8:25 a.m. in Bien Son commune, according to the ministry. (Vietnam-Soldiers)

TOKYO -- The Japanese government is considering a significant increase in defense spending over the next five years, with plans to raise the total defense budget for fiscal 2027 through 2031 to 60 trillion yen (about 376 billion U.S. dollars) when it revises the three key security documents, Kyodo News reported Friday, citing sources.
According to the report, spending focus will include large-scale procurement of drones, ammunition and missiles. (Japan-Defense-Budget)  ■

items.title: Explainer: How bomb threats are spooking Europe
text: ROME, Nov. 14 (Xinhua) -- A wave of hoax bomb threats targeting schools, airlines and media organizations has recently swept across Europe, disrupting public services and heightening security concerns.
As similar threats spill across national borders via hijacked email accounts and anonymous networks, European authorities face mounting pressure in identifying those responsible.
Though it remains unclear who is behind the threats hitting France, Spain, and other nations, European officials call them a coordinated effort to sow continent-wide confusion.
Regardless of who is responsible, how exactly are hoax bomb threats causing widespread disruption across Europe?

In Italy, around 6,300 schools received bomb threat emails on Wednesday, prompting widespread evacuations, while similar messages sent to schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland were dismissed as hoaxes.

The incidents followed a series of alerts involving European air travel in early November, when at least seven flights and a cruise ship were targeted in one incident, while nearly 30 passenger flights received hoax threats in another, prompting diversions, unplanned landings and fighter-jet escorts. Later, broadcasters in Ireland, Bulgaria and Britain were also targeted.
Across Europe, the threats caused widespread disruption, although no explosives were found and no injuries were reported.

The origins of the threats, however, remain unclear. An email sent to Italian schools was signed by a purported figure named "Mikhail Andropov," who also claimed responsibility for threats against newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria.

But the sender's identity remains unknown, and investigators have yet to establish whether the messages were linked to the threats against European flights. Authorities have not attributed the incidents to any group or state actor.

The threats could have been copycat incidents triggered by an initial alert, repeated actions by an individual or group, or hybrid warfare operations by state actors or their supporters, among several possible explanations outlined by Matthew Borie, co-founder and chief intelligence officer of Osprey Flight Solutions, which advises airlines on flight threats.

Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares described the incidents as a possible attempt at "hybrid aggression" and psychological warfare, arguing that the recurrence of similar incidents across Europe was unlikely to be mere coincidence.

He said cyberattacks on digital platforms and supermarket refrigeration systems also fit the pattern, in which hackers remotely manipulated temperature controls, causing refrigerators to warm up and food to spoil.

In Italy, the government said a special technical group would begin work on Friday to develop procedures and tools for responding to such threats in the short, medium, and long term. These measures would apply not only to schools but also to other potential targets.
Addressing such threats requires not only national-level preparedness but also closer coordination among European countries and institutions.

items.title: EU urges Israel to reopen all Gaza crossings, allow unimpeded humanitarian aid
text: BRUSSELS, Nov. 14 (Xinhua) -- The European Union (EU) on Saturday urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings to allow immediate, unimpeded access and sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale.

In a statement published by the European External Action Service (EEAS), the EU reiterated its grave concern over the persistent and devastating humanitarian crisis in Gaza. It said the severe flooding and winter conditions impacting the enclave are further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering.

The statement noted that a year after the ceasefire was announced, military strikes continue and shortages of essential items persist due to restricted access, resulting in the absence of acceptable and dignified living conditions.

The EU urged Israel to enable the work of the United Nations and its agencies, and humanitarian organizations, including non-governmental organizations, and to comply with all its obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law.

The bloc underlined the need to respect international law, including international humanitarian law, at all times, particularly the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as medical personnel and facilities. It described the recent airstrike on Nasser Hospital as "deeply alarming."

Reaffirming its commitment to the two-state solution, the EU called on all actors to fully implement the provisions of UN Security Council Resolution 2803 without delay, in line with relevant UN Security Council resolutions and international political and legal principles, in particular the permanent decommissioning of weapons from Hamas and other non-state armed groups, the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza and the civilian transition in Gaza.
The statement stressed that Hamas should not have any role in the future governance of Gaza.
On Nov. 7, Gaza's civil defense authorities declared a state of maximum emergency as a rainstorm flooded around 70,000 tents housing displaced Palestinians and overwhelmed rescue services.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, about 1.4 million Palestinians, or 65 percent of Gaza's population, were living in tents or makeshift shelters. It warned that humanitarian shelter stocks inside Gaza were virtually exhausted, while more than 150,000 tents remained outside the territory awaiting entry. However, Israel says it restricts certain materials over concerns that Hamas could use them for military purposes.  ■

China's independently developed 10-tonne electric aircraft completes first piloted flight
text: This photo taken on Nov. 14, 2026 shows the 10-tonne electric commercial aircraft CE-25A during its maiden piloted flight in Binzhou, east China's Shandong Province. China's independently developed 10-tonne electric commercial aircraft CE-25A completed its maiden piloted flight on Saturday, according to the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC). The aircraft carried two pilots and one flight-test engineer during the flight in Binzhou, east China's Shandong Province. The CE-25A is COMAC's first electric commercial aircraft. Designed mainly for intercity commercial flights, it can carry 19 passengers and has a maximum takeoff weight of 10 tonnes. It has a cruising speed of 300 km per hour, a cruising altitude of 2,400 meters and a range of 400 km. (Photo by Wang Jiliang/Xinhua)

SHANGHAI, Nov. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's independently developed 10-tonne electric commercial aircraft CE-25A completed its maiden piloted flight on Saturday, according to the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC).

The aircraft carried two pilots and one flight-test engineer during the flight in Binzhou, east China's Shandong Province. The aircraft operated normally, and all performance indicators met expectations, COMAC said.

The CE-25A is COMAC's first electric commercial aircraft. Designed mainly for intercity commercial flights, it can carry 19 passengers and has a maximum takeoff weight of 10 tonnes. It has a cruising speed of 300 km per hour, a cruising altitude of 2,400 meters and a range of 400 km.
The aircraft completed its first unmanned autonomous flight on Feb. 2 this year.
Developed jointly by COMAC, Chinese battery maker CATL, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and other partners, the CE-25A has completed 19 unmanned autonomous flight validations.
The Civil Aviation Administration of China has accepted COMAC's application for a type certificate. ■

APEC Primer in Four Words | Prosper: Decoding the APEC 2026 theme
text: APEC Primer in Four Words: The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 and 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." This four-part series unpacks four key words from that theme, one each day, to explain what APEC is and what the 2026 host year is about.
What does prosperity look like across 21 economies with vastly different populations, industries and levels of development?
For some, it means greater access to international markets. For others, it means stronger supply chains, new digital opportunities or growth that reaches more people.
Bringing those ambitions together is one of the central challenges facing APEC as China hosts the forum in 2026.

In the 2026 theme, prosperity is the goal and community-building is the means. That reflects APEC's long-term vision, the Putrajaya Vision 2040, which leaders adopted in 2020 under Malaysia's chairmanship. It calls for an "open, dynamic, resilient and peaceful" Asia-Pacific community by 2040, for the prosperity of all people and future generations.

When China introduced the 2026 theme and priorities in Shenzhen in December 2025, officials described the Asia-Pacific community not simply as an aspiration, but as something to be advanced through practical action. In that framing, openness, innovation and cooperation are the three priorities for turning the vision into concrete work.
The Putrajaya Vision identifies three broad economic drivers: trade and investment; innovation and digitalization; and strong, balanced, secure, sustainable and inclusive growth.

Together, those ideas suggest a broader definition of prosperity. It is not only about expanding trade or boosting output, but also about improving resilience, creating opportunities through technology, and making growth more widely shared.
That inclusive element is especially important in a forum as diverse as APEC, where member economies differ greatly in size, structure and stage of development.

APEC's own figures show that average tariffs among its member economies fell from 17 percent in 1989 to 5.3 percent in 2021. Meanwhile, its trade facilitation work from 2007 to 2010 helped cut regional trade transaction costs by 5 percent, generating estimated savings of $58.7 billion.

Those gains came largely from reducing traditional barriers. But the 2026 theme points to a wider set of tools. China has said it will actively expand the pathway for the building of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, and promote the formulation of a blueprint for upgrading connectivity.

A long-term vision needs a way to track progress. That is the role of the Aotearoa Plan of Action, which APEC leaders endorsed in 2021 during New Zealand's host year to implement the Putrajaya Vision 2040.

In 2026, APEC is carrying out the first scheduled five-year review of the plan's collective actions. The process is designed to assess what has been done so far and consider which actions should be continued, revised or updated as the forum works toward its 2040 goal.

items.title: Feature: From seed to cup, Ethiopian coffee gains popularity in China
text: ADDIS ABABA, Nov. 14 (Xinhua) -- Scattered in the misty, yet sun-drenched highlands of southwestern Ethiopia, premium organic coffee cherries are hand-picked, sun-dried, and carefully processed before they embark on a long journey to China, where a rapidly growing appetite for specialty coffee is cementing an expanding commercial bridge between the two nations.
Every morning, Alemu Haile steps into the lush expanse of Awo Coffee's 200-hectare plantation in the Gimbo District of the southwest region of Ethiopia to oversee coffee growing and processing.

"My daily routine involves coordinating the hand-picking of coffee cherries, ensuring that workers carefully select only the vibrant red cherries at the absolute peak of their ripeness," Haile told Xinhua in a recent interview. He emphasized that balancing the proper amount of sunlight for the coffee trees is critical to ensure the cherries ripen uniformly during the harvest season, which normally falls in October.

Once harvested, the cherries move to post-processing under Haile's supervision, where trained personnel perform rigorous manual sorting to filter out immature, insect-damaged and deformed beans. To guarantee export standards, the farm also deploys a water flotation technique that instantly separates and discards any inherently inferior beans, ensuring only top-tier selections advance to the long, raised drying beds.

The sun-drying and processing phase, which often lasts for three weeks, is also considered a "very critical stage," mainly because coffee beans readily absorb tastes and aromas from their surroundings. To ensure quality, Haile excercises maximum caution to protect the sensitive beans from dust, soil, or any other external exposure.
Much of this meticulously processed high-quality coffee is subsequently shipped to China by Awo Coffee, one of Ethiopia's fast-growing coffee processors and exporters.

Named after the Amharic word for "Yes," Awo Coffee began its exports to China about 12 years ago right when the business was founded. The company has since witnessed a steadily expanding market presence in China, with annual shipments surging from modest tens of tonnes to over 200 tonnes last year, the company's General Manager Tesfaye Gebru told Xinhua.

To address evolving consumer preferences in China, Kaleab Fekad, Awo Coffee's marketing manager, noted that the company has in recent years diversified its product offerings beyond raw beans to include roasted options and packaged powdered coffee, sourced both from its own farm and through collaborations with smallholder farmers.

"Since we began exporting raw coffee beans and later expanded into processed and powdered coffee, our export figures have grown rapidly and at a very large scale over the years. Our brand is also getting more and more awareness among Chinese consumers," Fekad said.

Looking ahead, Awo Coffee has formulated comprehensive growth plans aimed at scaling up its operational capacity in China, while honoring its rich heritage of authentic Ethiopian premium Arabica coffee flavor profiles.

items.title: China's yuan loans grow 11.42 trln yuan in first 10 months
text: BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 11.42 trillion yuan (about 1.7 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first 10 months of 2026, central bank data showed on Friday.
At the end of October, outstanding yuan loans stood at 283.33 trillion yuan, up 4.7 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China (PBOC).
China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 469.16 trillion yuan at the end of October, up 7.2 percent year on year, the central bank noted.
M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, increased by 7.1 percent year on year to 359.06 trillion yuan by the end of last month, the PBOC said.

"Growth rates of M2 and total social financing remained at reasonable levels, creating an appropriate monetary and financial environment for economic recovery and upgrading," said Zhou Zhen, associate professor at Tsinghua University's PBC School of Finance.

Credit has flowed increasingly to key areas. In the first 10 months, loans to enterprises and public institutions increased by 12.39 trillion yuan, including 6.69 trillion yuan in medium- and long-term loans.

Outstanding inclusive loans to small and micro businesses rose 6.9 percent year on year to 38.24 trillion yuan. Outstanding medium- and long-term loans to the service sector, excluding the real estate sector, rose 9.2 percent to 62.99 trillion yuan. Both outpaced overall loan growth.
By the end of September, some 307,300 small and medium-sized sci-tech enterprises had received loan support, with a loan access rate of 51.1 percent.
Financing channels have become more diversified. In the first 10 months, bond and equity financing accounted for around 53 percent of new aggregate social financing.

Funding costs remained low this year. In October, the weighted average rate on newly issued enterprise loans was about 2.9 percent, down 0.2 percentage points year on year, while that on new personal housing loans was about 3.1 percent, basically unchanged from the same period last year.

Zhang Xu, an analyst at Everbright Securities, said that as the integrated effects of existing and new policies continue to emerge, the financial system will keep providing strong support for the high-quality development of the real economy.

items.title: China's 590-year-old pickle maker finds wider market
text: A staff member displays boxes of sesame peanut butter ice cream and black garlic ice cream at a store of Liubiju in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Ju Huanzong)

BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- For generations, Beijing families have bought Liubiju's sweet pickled garlic to go with hotpot and sweet bean sauce to accompany roast duck. These days, customers at the company's historic Qianmen store can also find peanut-sesame-paste ice cream, vinegar slushies and freshly baked pastries flavored with traditional Chinese condiments.

The new offerings would have been hard to imagine at Liubiju a few years ago, when the 590-year-old food maker was struggling to stay afloat. After losing more than 15 million yuan (about 2.23 million U.S. dollars) in 2021, the company returned to profit, earning over 26 million yuan in 2025, its best result in decades. The recovery followed an overhaul of its products, sales channels and management.

Liubiju's experience offers a window into how China's traditional brands are responding to changing consumer habits. The country's total retail sales of consumer goods rose 1.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026, while online food sales grew 15.8 percent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

Founded in 1436, Liubiju had long relied on the appeal of its pickled vegetables and sauces, products closely associated with Beijing cuisine but less familiar elsewhere in China. Their production also imposed limits on growth.

At its factory in southern Beijing, more than 2,000 earthenware vats stand in neat rows, half-buried in the ground. Workers use long wooden paddles to stir the vegetables and sauce, turning loads weighing 50 kilograms or more. The company's sweet pickled garlic undergoes roughly 150 days of fermentation, during which workers must repeatedly roll the sealed jars by hand.
Such labor-intensive methods help preserve Liubiju's distinctive flavors, but leave little room to increase production at short notice.
Staff members make pickled products at a workshop of Liubiju in Beijing, capital of China, March 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiao)

When Yu Jiangfu joined Liubiju as marketing director in 2020, the company's core business had been losing money for years, with rental income helping cover the shortfall. Many younger consumers knew Liubiju sold pickles but had little idea of what kinds. The company had kept adding products in an attempt to revive sales, eventually amassing more than 900 items without improving profitability.

Yu, now the general manager of Liubiju, recalled that the company faced a stark question: "Could this time-honored brand even survive?" His team cut the product range from more than 900 items at its peak to fewer than 300, retaining traditional staples such as pickles, soybean pastes and rice vinegar while selectively introducing new products.

A native of coastal Fujian Province in east China, Yu saw limited prospects for traditional northern Chinese pickles in the country's southern markets, where tastes differed. A sauce used in a variety of everyday dishes, however, seemed a more promising bet.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop after thousands of flights disrupted
text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after hours of disruption affected thousands of flights across the country.
Flight cancellations and delays are expected to continue through the weekend.

At a press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the country's "incredibly old" air traffic control system for the nationwide ground stop. He asked Congress for 50 billion U.S. dollars in emergency funding to overhaul the aging air traffic control infrastructure.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, who was also at the press conference Friday evening, said that while nothing was completely certain at that point, there were no indications that a cyberattack was responsible.
Earlier, Duffy said on the social media platform X that the FAA had issued the nationwide ground stop following a "communication issue" impacting all air route traffic control centers.
U.S. media reported that the FAA had issued an advisory citing "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety" as grounds for the nationwide ground stop, describing it as a rare move.
More than 10,000 flights were disrupted, according to a report by CNBC, which noted that more flight cancellations were expected to extend into Saturday.

U.S. President Donald Trump said the nationwide ground stop does not appear to be the result of a cyberattack or artificial intelligence, according to Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy.

"It doesn't seem like that," Doocy told "The Ingraham Angle" after speaking with Trump by phone. Trump believed that the disruption appeared to stem from "a bunch of old broken stuff" that the FAA relies on to keep air travel operating.

Earlier on Friday, Eurocontrol said that all flights departing from its member states for U.S. airports were suspended at the request of the FAA. The suspension covers departures between 2200 GMT on Friday and 0500 GMT on Saturday.
The U.S. nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

items.title: Chinese EV connects German drivers, opens doors to greater cooperation
text: A vehicle on display is seen at the booth of Chinese automaker Aito during the 2026 Paris Motor Show in Paris, France, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo)

While German brands remain firmly established in the domestic market, the country's roads are becoming more diverse, with European and Asian manufacturers gaining ground. Chinese EV brands, in particular, are becoming increasingly visible.

REGENSBURG, Germany, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- On Oct. 3, Germany's Unity Day, German software engineer Renick Buettner set off in his NIO EL7, an electric SUV made by Chinese automaker NIO, for the Bavarian city of Regensburg, where NIO owners gather on a Saturday each month to share their experiences and enthusiasm for the Chinese electric vehicle (EV) brand.
At 27, Buettner grew up in Germany's car-loving culture and has driven a range of European and American brands. Today, however, two Chinese electric vehicles have found a place in his garage.
What won him over was not simply the price or the brand, but how naturally the cars fit into his daily life. "I want a simple, intelligent experience," Buettner told Xinhua during the drive.
As the automotive industry shifts toward electrification and intelligent mobility, his priorities have evolved, with software, intelligent cockpits and ease of use becoming increasingly important.

"Many of the smart features in Chinese electric vehicles are seamlessly integrated into the driving experience. They simplify tasks that would otherwise require manual operation and make the car a more natural part of everyday life," he said.
People visit the booth of Chinese automaker Forthing during the 2026 Paris Motor Show in Paris, France, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo)

His impressions are based on firsthand experience. During a road trip to China this spring, Buettner attended events showcasing new models from Chinese automakers and test-drove several vehicles. He was particularly impressed by their interior design and intelligent features, which he found offered a different approach from that of German brands.

For instance, drivers can use navigation systems to locate specific types of charging stations, control vehicle functions through voice commands and adjust the air conditioning with an intelligent in-car assistant. "Once you have been to China and driven these cars yourself, you see things differently," he said.
Buettner's experience reflects a broader shift in Germany, a country long renowned for its automotive engineering and home to some of the world's leading carmakers.

While German brands remain firmly established in the domestic market, the country's roads are becoming more diverse, with European and Asian manufacturers gaining ground. Chinese EV brands, in particular, are becoming increasingly visible.

items.title: BBNJ Secretariat decision should best serve the oceans and all humanity
text:
By Li Yang | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-15 20:04

On Nov 6, without consulting the Parties to the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), Belgium and Chile announced their decision to join their candidatures for the location of the Secretariat and the Clearing-House Mechanism.

Their joint candidature, which proposes the Secretariat to be based in the city of Valparaiso, Chile, the CHM to operate from Brussels, with meetings of subsidiary bodies also to be held in the Belgian capital, is an attempt to hijack the collective will of the parties. As Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said, the arrangement is an unauthorized backroom deal that risks turning a multilateral selection process into a problematic bilateral bargain.

The BBNJ Agreement came into force in January, marking an important advance in global ocean governance. Its implementation is supposed to embody the principles of international cooperation, equitable participation and the rule of law. The Belgium-Chile proposal violates the stipulations of the Agreement and disrespects the authority of the Conference of the Parties, as Mao rightly pointed out.

Decisions regarding the location of the Secretariat, CHM arrangements and venues for subsidiary-body meetings must be made by the COP. They are not bargaining chips to be bundled into a package and presented to other parties as a fait accompli. The proposed separation of the Secretariat and CHM across continents also raises practical concerns. Since the CHM is a core component of the Secretariat's responsibilities, splitting their locations could increase operational costs, complicate coordination and impose unnecessary financial burdens on the parties.

There is also a question of geographical equity. Brussels already hosts major international institutions, including the European Union and NATO. Locating an important component of the ocean-governance framework in the Belgian capital, while excluding Asia from hosting any major global institution of comparable standing, such as the BBNJ Secretariat, would only exacerbate the longstanding geographical imbalance in international governance. For developing countries, particularly those in the Global South, the issue is whether multilateral institutions genuinely reflect the interests and participation of the wider international community.

The rationale of the so-called joint candidacy also raises questions. Chile initially framed its bid as an opportunity to strengthen the Global South's voice in ocean governance. Under the new proposal, however, it would host the Secretariat without assuming responsibility for the CHM, while Belgium would secure the latter and host subsidiary-body meetings. Such a division risks subordinating institutional effectiveness and equitable geographical representation to diplomatic deal-making.

items.title: Chinese folk music concert bridges cultures in Nairobi
text: A concert featuring traditional Chinese musical instruments took place in Nairobi, Kenya, on Saturday as part of the Kenya International Theatre Festival. The performance brought together leading Chinese folk instrumentalists and vocalists, showcasing traditional Chinese instruments including the guqin, erhu, zhongruan, and suona.

The concert opened with a joint performance by musicians from the Beijing Golden Bell Star Chinese Chamber Orchestra and the African Women's Orchestra from Kenya. Bringing the evening to a close, the Chinese musicians performed Jambo Bwana, a popular Swahili song, on traditional Chinese instruments, drawing warm applause from the audience.

items.title: 12 leaders of APEC economies to attend APEC CEO Summit 2026
text: SHENZHEN -- Twelve leaders of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies will attend the APEC CEO Summit 2026, which is scheduled to be held from Nov 17 to 18 in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong province, the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade said Sunday.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, along with leaders from APEC economies Australia, Canada, Chile, China's Hong Kong, Indonesia, the Republic of Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, Russia, Thailand and Vietnam, will attend the summit and deliver speeches or remarks, or participate in panel discussions, said Li Qingshuang, vice-chairperson of the CCPIT, at a news conference.

items.title: Russian troops seize settlement of Tersyanka in southeast Ukraine
text: MOSCOW -- Russian forces have captured the settlement of Tersyanka in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporozhye region and taken control of a Ukrainian fortified area spanning more than 10 square kilometers, the Russian Defense Ministry said Saturday.
Assault units seized the settlement and cleared more than 300 buildings, the ministry said, according to TASS news agency.
The Ukrainian armed forces lost more than 1,000 troops in the special military operation zone over the past 24 hours as a result of operations by Russian battle groups, the report said.

China's independently developed 10-ton electric aircraft completes first piloted flight
text: SHANGHAI -- China's independently developed 10-ton electric commercial aircraft CE-25A completed its maiden piloted flight on Saturday, according to the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC).

The aircraft carried two pilots and one flight-test engineer during the flight in Binzhou, East China's Shandong province. The aircraft operated normally, and all performance indicators met expectations, COMAC said.

The CE-25A is COMAC's first electric commercial aircraft. Designed mainly for intercity commercial flights, it can carry 19 passengers and has a maximum takeoff weight of 10 metric tons. It has a cruising speed of 300 km per hour, a cruising altitude of 2,400 meters and a range of 400 km.
The aircraft completed its first unmanned autonomous flight on Feb 2 this year.
Developed jointly by COMAC, Chinese battery maker CATL, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and other partners, the CE-25A has completed 19 unmanned autonomous flight validations.
The Civil Aviation Administration of China has accepted COMAC's application for a type certificate.

items.title: COMAC's electric aircraft completes first piloted test flight
text: China's first domestically developed 10-metric-ton-class electric commercial aircraft, the CE-25A, completed its first piloted test flight in Binzhou, Shandong province, on Saturday, marking another milestone in the development of electric aircraft for short-haul commercial travel.

The aircraft, developed by Commercial Aircraft Corp of China, carried two pilots and a flight test engineer. The test lasted 57 minutes and 46 seconds, including 16 minutes and 38 seconds in the air, during which the aircraft covered 60.4 kilometers.
The aircraft performed normally and all test results met expectations, COMAC said in a statement.

The CE-25A is COMAC's first electric commercial aircraft, designed to carry 19 passengers on commercial flights between cities. It has a maximum takeoff weight of 10 metric tons, a cruising speed of 300 kilometers per hour, a cruising altitude of 2,400 meters, and a range of 400 kilometers.
The aircraft is powered by a distributed electric ducted-fan propulsion system mounted on its wings.

items.title: CSG brings energy transition solutions to COP31 China Pavilion
text: A thematic side event titled "Digital-Intelligent Innovation for Green Electricity: Building a New Power System and New Practices for Global Energy Transition" was held in Antalya, Turkiye, on Nov 13 local time, on the sidelines of the China Pavilion at COP31, officially known as the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.

The event was guided by China's National Energy Administration, hosted by China Southern Power Grid (CSG), and co-organized by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) and the Office for China-IRENA Cooperation (China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute).

Through the release of research findings, roundtable discussions and case studies, the side event showcased Chinese energy companies' innovative exploration and international practices in building a new power system, contributing Chinese expertise and solutions to the global low-carbon energy transition.

Liu Zhenmin, China's special envoy for climate change, Francesco La Camera, director-general of IRENA, Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana, under-secretary-general of the United Nations and executive secretary of the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), Xiong Minfeng, deputy director-general of the Department of International Cooperation under National Energy Administration of China, attended the event and delivered opening remarks.

At the side event, CSG, aligning with the broader context of global energy transition and climate governance, presented its achievements in building a new power system through systematic innovation practices.

A highlight of the event was the joint release by CSG, IRENA and the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute of "Solutions for building a new power system: The role of grids, storage and hydropower". The report systematically reviews the technical requirements arising from high shares of renewable energy and increasing electrification, and introduces solutions and practical experience from early-moving countries.

The Global Energy Storage Alliance Initiative was officially launched by CSG Energy Storage, the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute and the China Energy Storage Alliance, together with leading domestic and international enterprises, with several international institutions and industry organizations expressing their intention to join.
As a representative unit of the alliance, CSG Energy Storage outlined how advances in energy storage can support the development of new power systems.

CSG released for the first time the Chinese and English editions of the CSG White Paper on Green Development, comprehensively presenting the company's achievements during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25) in clean energy supply, green and low-carbon operations, and electricity-carbon coupling business, and outlining plans to further develop three key areas — a new power system, new energy systems, and a new-type power grid — during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30).

items.title: Weekend Long Read: ‘Unseen Paintings’ Exhibition Reimagines Chinese Landscapes
text: At the Red Brick Art Museum in Beijing, the new exhibition Bingyi: Unseen Paintings is not an easy show to get into.

The exhibition is more than a solo retrospective of the artist Bingyi. It points to a shift in how East and West exchange ideas about art. For decades, Western art history set the terms, favoring defined, formed images, an aesthetic known as Qian, the yang principle. Chinese landscape painting, or “shanshui,” stood for Kun, the yin force of creation, rooted in inner contemplation rather than geometric observation.

items.title: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
text: An AI-generated short drama made by amateurs, including a former rideshare driver and a stay-at-home mother, has gone viral in China for its high production quality and historical accuracy, challenging the genre’s reputation for simple, brainless plots.

First released in August, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” already has 10 seasons and comprises roughly 1,000 3-minute episodes. As of Thursday, the show has amassed over 12 billion views across platforms including Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, and streaming site Bilibili, local media reported.

In the first nine months of this year, 490,000 micro-dramas were released in China, 13 times more than in all of 2025. AI is also reshaping the micro-drama industry, with AI-generated productions now accounting for more than 90% of all such content, according to a report the National Radio and Television Administration released in October. The report also found that China’s short-drama audience had surpassed 600 million active monthly viewers.

Adapted from a web novel published in installments beginning this April by a writer under the pen name Chagen’er, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” follows five modern-day soldiers who unwittingly travel back to the late Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), bringing their weapons and military expertise with them.

The late Northern Song period is a popular setting for Chinese time-travel fiction, as it offers viewers an alternative reality to the dynasty’s end, when invading Jurchen tribes captured two of its emperors — widely remembered as a national disgrace.

Fans have praised the drama’s carefully crafted script, elaborate fight scenes, and rounded characters who grapple with everything from the imperial examination system to weapons, food, and military equipment shortages during invasions by northern nomadic groups.
The historical details have prompted some viewers to look up Song-era official ranks, military organizations, and historical records and compare them against the drama’s depictions.

The production team behind “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” reportedly comprises six members — including a former pharmaceutical sales representative, interior designer, rideshare driver, stay-at-home mother, and wholesale business owner — who met during an online course on how to use AI to make short dramas.

Zhang Hansheng, 54, the production team’s head, told domestic media that the series has so far cost roughly 1 million yuan ($150,000) to produce, but declined to disclose the team’s earnings. However, rumors of hefty returns have drawn fresh attention to AI drama production, which many see as a potential source of new opportunities for grassroots content creators.

In the comments on a video interview with Zhang by the domestic outlet Yicai, some viewers said the project had inspired them to learn AI tools and try making dramas themselves. Others urged caution, noting the rise of scams disguised as AI-related courses.

The show’s success comes as the genre shifts toward higher production values. Until recently, short dramas were widely considered mindless entertainment defined by exaggerated interpersonal conflicts, formulaic characters, and implausible plots.

items.title: How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019263/How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
text: Editor’s note: Zhang Li is a professor of anthropology at the University of California, Davis, and the author of “Anxious China: Inner Revolution and Politics of Psychotherapy,” which explores how a new psychotherapeutic culture is taking root in China amid profound socioeconomic change. A Chinese version of the book was released this summer. Here, Zhang, who grew up in Kunming, capital of the southwestern Yunnan province, talks with The Paper about her personal journey, trends in mental health care, and the potential impact of artificial intelligence.

The Paper: In your book, you say that returning home to Kunming to conduct research into the city’s mental and psychological landscape was a “deeply emotional experience” that sometimes left you feeling vulnerable. How did your personal connection with Kunming shape this project?

Zhang: The idea for the book first came to me when I learned that my best friend from middle school had become a therapist. I was quite surprised. This was around 2000, when interest in psychology was just beginning to take off in China and few people knew anything about mental health counseling. When I talked to my friend about her work, I realized that it touched on all kinds of everyday issues but was relatively unexplored. Most of the anthropological field research I’d come across had been conducted outside China.

As I worked on the project, I discovered how deeply it was connected to my family. My mother died 13 years ago. Looking back, I realized she’d lived with post-traumatic stress disorder for much of her life. She lost her mother when she was 8 years old. Her father remarried, and her stepmother treated her and her siblings very badly.

Growing up, we became accustomed to her extreme emotional reactions, but we had no idea they were symptomatic of a psychological disorder. Back then, people simply described this behavior as having “a bad temper.” It was only after reading up on the subject that I came to understand that my mother had suffered from chronic anxiety and depression, but she lacked the language to express it.

Seeing a psychiatrist is more normalized now; back then, mental health was a taboo topic. When I began my fieldwork, my mother was 80. I repeatedly urged her to see a psychiatrist, and eventually she agreed. After a complicated and rather haphazard diagnostic process, she was prescribed a short course of Prozac, which helped improve her condition. In the final three years of her life, she was relatively at peace, and we could have calmer, more constructive conversations.

I chose Kunming for my fieldwork because it allowed me to leverage personal connections and familiarity with the local environment. In addition, scholars were already conducting similar research in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai, so I wanted to look at a medium-sized city. Kunming was experiencing many of the same problems as larger cities amid China’s economic reforms and social transformation. Rapid, large-scale change inevitably causes disruption, and the psychological disruption individuals experience manifests in all kinds of ways.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
text: SHANGHAI — When prospective clients contacted Li Shuping’s medical companion agency in Shanghai, their first question often had little to do with the hospital visit they were arranging.

“Patients used to ask first whether we were individuals or a legitimate agency,” Li tells Sixth Tone. Patients hire her company, Qingbeihu, to send a trained companion with them to hospital, helping with appointments, consultations, and paperwork.

The agency opened in September 2025, when almost anyone could advertise the same service on social media. And with people aged 60 or older accounting for 23% of China’s population by the end of 2025 and 59 million forecast to need care by 2030, more families were turning to companions to guide elderly relatives through hospital visits.

But written contracts were often absent, leaving services and fees unclear. Some patients faced unexpected charges once a visit was underway, with little recourse if they disputed them, prompting calls for tighter oversight.

But since Shanghai announced new rules for medical companion services effective July 1, Qingbeihu has received more inquiries, Li says. “Orders are growing steadily, and prospective clients seem more willing to trust the service.”

The rules cover medical companion services for Shanghai residents aged 60 and older and set requirements for worker qualifications, pricing transparency, and written contracts. They also require companions to wear identity badges, provide public lists of qualified agencies, and define responsibilities that include helping patients communicate with doctors and offering psychological support.

More recently, a national standard that took effect Nov. 1 covers medical companion services for patients of all ages across China. It also sets limits on what companions can do, prohibiting them from giving medical advice or making treatment decisions on patients’ behalf.

Following Shanghai’s new rules, Li says Qingbeihu now uses written risk and privacy agreements with patients and companions, as well as accident insurance for companions. For elderly clients unfamiliar with digital services, the agency also provides paper consent forms before a visit.
“Elderly people are very willing to have young people accompany them to seek care — it is also a kind of emotional support,” Li says.
For Qingbeihu’s six full-time companions, all under 30, the working day often begins as early as 5 a.m.

By the time Li Suyu, not related to Li Shuping, meets a patient at the hospital around 7:30 a.m., she has already asked about their medical history, drug allergies, and mobility. She then checks registration details and organizes medical records and examination reports before the hospital opens at 8.

Once consultations begin, the 22-year-old accompanies patients to see their doctors, records treatment plans and prescribed medications, and arranges any examinations ordered. She also keeps family members informed and, after the visit, helps patients keep track of follow-up appointments and medication reminders.

items.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
text: A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.
“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.
The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”
Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.
In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.
Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.
He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
text: Fufeng County, some 110 kilometers west of the northwestern Chinese city of Xi’an, is best known for its stunning Tang dynasty (618–907) relics, unearthed from an underground crypt beneath Famen Temple in the late 1980s.

But ask a Chinese archaeologist about Fufeng, and they’ll likely point you in another direction: toward a quiet cluster of more than 20 villages located along the border with neighboring Qishan County. There, hidden beneath unassuming farms and village houses, lies what a growing number of experts believe was the first capital of the Western Zhou (1046–771 BC) — one of China’s earliest and most important dynasties.

Known as Zhouyuan — literally “The Plains of Zhou” — its excavation sites have produced some of China’s most famous bronze ritual vessels. In the 1940s, those discoveries led archaeologist Shi Zhangru to survey the area and eventually propose that this was Qiyi, the center of Zhou culture before the Zhou toppled the Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC).

In the decades that followed, archaeologists worked on the site sporadically, uncovering large rammed-earth building foundations, cemeteries, craft workshops, bronze hoards, and oracle bones, all dating to the Zhou period.

Yet planned, continuous excavation at Zhouyuan began only at the turn of the 21st century, when the Institute of Archaeology at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, and Peking University’s School of Archaeology and Museology formed a joint team to systematically explore the site.

Why the delay? Part of the problem was historiographical. Chinese scholars have long relied on written texts to locate historic sites, and for more than 2,000 years historians placed the Western Zhou capital dozens of kilometers away, in a place called Fenghao, near Xi’an.

This drew attention and resources from other sites in the region, including Zhouyuan. But over the past decade or so, the joint archaeological team at Zhouyuan has made a string of breakthroughs that suggest Shi Zhangru’s near-century-old hunch might be right — and possibly even show that Zhouyuan, not Fenghao, was the Western Zhou’s first capital.

“Modern excavations are revealing more and more contradictions between the archaeological record and traditional accounts,” Cao Dazhi, a Peking University-based archaeologist and co-leader of the Zhouyuan team, wrote in a 2023 paper. Cao’s analysis attracted widespread attention in China for arguing that Zhouyuan was the Zhou capital, while the Fenghao region was merely an important hub and site of the royal hunting grounds.
But the dispute over ancient capitals may not be the biggest revelation to emerge from the Zhouyuan excavations.

While the exact significance of the discoveries remains a matter of debate even within the team, mounting evidence suggests the Zhou capital’s population was far more diverse than previously thought. In addition to the core Zhou population, it was home to large numbers of conquered Shang, as well as migrants from the northwest and south.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
text: “Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.
“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”
“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.
Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.
(Header image: Urinals installed in a women’s restroom at a bar in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

Philippines, Australia sign defence pact with eye on China
text: MANILA — The Philippines and Australia signed a defence cooperation arrangement on Sunday that Manila said ​would lower bureaucratic hurdles to joint military activities, as the two countries ‌further deepen security ties.

Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the arrangement would streamline implementation of the bilateral Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, or SOVFA, by simplifying coordination procedures.
“Rather than 100 steps to do ​a single thing, it will just now take 10,” Teodoro told reporters, ​describing the deal as an “anti-red tape measure” for implementing SOVFA.

He said the ⁠arrangement would pave the way for closer cooperation involving maritime, air and land ​forces, as well as humanitarian and disaster response, and would bolster the Philippines’ “credible deterrence posture”, ​including in the South China Sea.
China’s defence and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent on Sunday.

The Philippines has been broadening its network of security ties while complementing a ​long-standing alliance with its treaty partner, the United States, in the face of ​what it describes as China’s aggressive behaviour in the South China Sea, where countries have overlapping maritime ‌claims.

Australia ⁠has consistently supported Manila’s position on the strategic waterway, backing a 2016 ruling by an international arbitral tribunal that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.
